result.summary: Pausanias arrives at Sparta and describes its market-place, public offices and monuments, including the Persian Portico and temples of Caesar and Augustus. He tells the story of the seer Agias and his ancestor Tisamenus, then lists statues, temples and tombs, including that of Orestes.

scenes.title: Arrival and Spartan market-place
scenes.summary: Pausanias reaches Sparta, states his method, and describes the market-place offices, the Persian Portico and the temples of Caesar and Augustus.

scenes.title: Agias and Tisamenus the seer
scenes.summary: Pausanias tells how Agias foretold Lysander's victory, and how his ancestor Tisamenus won five victories for Sparta as the oracle foretold.
scenes.stakes: Tisamenus risks missing the oracle's promised victories; the Spartans risk defeat in their wars.

place.name: Ægos-potamoi, Olympia, Platæa and other battlefields

scenes.title: Statues, temples and tombs
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the Dance-ground, temples, the tomb of Orestes and other monuments around the market-place.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias states his method of selecting only the most remarkable details.

analysis.text: The Persian Portico, built from spoils of the Persian Wars, shows how Sparta remembered its victories in civic architecture.
Pausanias blends monuments with local tradition, such as oracles and tombs, to present Sparta's religious and political identity.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias writes under Roman rule, so he explains Augustus by giving the Greek equivalent Sebastus.

language_notes.text: The Bidiæi were a board of five Spartan magistrates who supervised the young men's exercises and contests.
Eponymus: the magistrate whose name was used to date the year, as the archon did at Athens.
Autocracy means rule by a single person; here it refers to the Roman imperial government.
Sebastus is Greek for 'revered' or 'august', the standard Greek rendering of the title Augustus.
Ægos-potamoi (405 BC) was the battle where Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet, ending the Peloponnesian War.
The pentathlum was the Olympic pentathlon: running, leaping, discus, javelin and wrestling.
The Gymnopædia was a Spartan festival where boys danced and exercised unclad, honouring Apollo and commemorating fallen warriors.
Epimenides was a legendary Cretan seer and purifier, said to have cleansed Athens of plague.

context_notes.text: Mardonius commanded the Persian army and was killed at Platæa in 479 BC, so the Portico celebrates that Greek victory.
The Iamidæ were a famous Elean family of seers, descended from the prophet Iamus.
Orestes, son of Agamemnon, was a mythical figure whose bones, by tradition, were moved to Sparta as an oracle commanded.

literary_notes.text: The firm, personal declaration of method shows Pausanias as a selective, authoritative guide.
Tisamenus lost the Olympic contest yet the oracle was fulfilled differently, so the apparent failure reveals its true meaning.
